newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh Monno Ceramic Industry shut after attack.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh Monno Ceramic Industry shut after attack.

text.p: Bangladesh's Monno Ceramic Industry Ltd's operations have been shut down indefinitely after workers ransacked its factory over a labour dispute, company officials said on Wednesday.
They said the factory at Dhamrai near Dhaka had been closed since Sunday. Police were investigating, one official said.

Monno, which makes tableware, tops Bangladesh's export-led ceramics sector with an increasing presence in overseas markets. Its tableware exports in 1995/96 (July-June) earned 363.1 million taka ($8.3 million), up nearly 75 million taka from the previous year, the officials said.

"We were forced to shut down the factory. A section of unruly labourers ransacked the factory, its offices and attacked living quarters of foreign engineers," said M.H. Khan, chairman and managing director of the company.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has asked law and order agencies to investigate the incident.
"I met the prime minister on Tuesday and she asked the Home Minister to address the situation on an emergency basis. She termed the industry as a national pride," Khan told Reuters on Wednesday.
The Bangladesh Ceramic Wares Manufacturers' Association, at an emergency meeting on Tuesday, urged the Home Ministry to take immediate measures to save the Monno Ceramics factory.
The United States is Monno's largest buyer, taking 27 percent of its export turnover. Other major buyers include Italy, Britain, Spain, France, New Zealand, Australia, Netherlands and Argentina.

Monno Ceramic Industry Ltd started production in January 1985 and went public that year. Its paid-up capital increased to 135 million taka in June 1996 from 90 million a year ago after the company offered 450,000 bonus shares of 100 taka each in 1994/95.
Monno's share price has been sliding since its factory was shut down, dropping nearly 67 taka to 748 on Tuesday and losing 39 taka to 815 on Monday.
Some 30 people including police were injured during the weekend labour unrest, one official said.
"Some self declared trade union leaders led the attack as they had been suspended for their illegal action. They were abstaining from duties," Khan said.
"They were pressing me to increase their wages and trying to gain other benefits without working."
But Iqbal Azad, a leader of the workers, denied the allegations. "The authority suspended our colleagues without following the trade union law," he told Reuters.
The President of the Federation of Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI), Yusuf Abdullah Harun, expressed deep concern over the attack on the factory.
"Such incidents will definitely have an adverse effect both on domestic as well as foreign direct investment," he said.
Police said security forces were patrolling the factory premises on Wednesday. ($1 = 43.65 taka)
